1026-the-diary-of-a-nobody:
Charles Pooter is a London clerk of modest means. He keeps a diary of small triumphs and mishaps: a new house in the suburbs, a dinner that goes wrong, and a son who will not behave. George Grossmith and his brother Weed wrote this comic novel as a string of daily entries, and it first ran in Punch.

Pooter's pride, his snobbery, and his knack for mishap make him both a joke and a figure of real warmth. Friends mock him, tradesmen vex him, and each slight looms large in his pages. The diary made "Pooter" a byword for the well-meaning little man, and it still charms readers with its deadpan wit.
10358-the-boss-of-little-arcady:
Harry Leon Wilson published this comic novel in 1905, set in a small Midwestern town he calls Little Arcady. Its boss is Colonel Potts, a grand talker whose golden day, love affairs, and mad pranks rule the town's talk. Wilson tells the tale in two books, one for Potts and one for Miss Caroline.

A sleuth named Billy Durgin, a lady of powers, a catastrophe in furniture, and troubled waters stilled fill the comic plot. Dreams, fabling, and town gossip carry the humor. Readers get a warm, funny portrait of small-town America, with a hero who charms even when he blunders.
10639-phrases-for-public-speakers-and-pa:
Grenville Kleiser compiled Phrases for Public Speakers and Paragraphs for Study in 1910 as a book of practice, not theory. He argues that skilled speakers rely on hundreds of ready phrases that hold thought together and allow fluent speech at short notice. Students are told to read pages aloud daily, think through each phrase, and recast it in their own words.

The second half reprints paragraphs from notable speeches, so learners can study climax, rhythm, and force in real examples. A month of earnest practice, Kleiser promises, brings striking gains. Speakers, students, and debaters still find it a handy drill book for building ease and fluency on one's feet.
10847-the-maids-tragedy:
Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher's The Maid's Tragedy is a Jacobean tragedy of love, honor, and revenge at court. Its persons include the King, his brother Lysippus, Amintor the noble gentleman, Evadne his wife, her brothers Melantius and Diphilus, and Aspatia, Amintor's troth-plight wife. A masque opens the first act, with lords debating poetry and show.

The plot turns on a forced marriage, a king's lust, and vows broken and kept, driving toward violence. Beaumont and Fletcher write in high, passionate verse. Readers meet one of the most famous tragedies of Shakespeare's age, still staged for its plot and poetry.
1191-the-double-dealer-a-comedy:
William Congreve's second comedy turns on Maskwell, a villain who smiles at all sides while betraying each. He plots to steal his friend's bride and fortune, juggling lovers, wives, and patrons with cool deceit. The play's intrigues twist until Maskwell's own web traps him.

Congreve writes the Restoration stage at its most cynical, with dialogue that cuts like a rapier. The comedy is darker than Love for Love, and its villain is its star. The play draws readers who like sharp talk and plots where no one is quite innocent.
1192-the-old-bachelor-a-comedy:
William Congreve's first comedy, staged in 1693, follows Bellmour and Vainlove, two fashionable rakes, as they pursue the witty Belinda and Araminta through a maze of letters, masks, and false vows. The Old Bachelor of the title, Heartwell, a professed woman-hater, falls hardest of all.

The play's talk is fast, polished, and full of Restoration bite, and its plot turns on who can outwit whom in love. Congreve was barely twenty when he wrote it. The comedy still pleases readers who like sharp dialogue and the manners of late Stuart London.
1244-love-for-love-a-comedy:
William Congreve's comedy of 1695 follows Valentine, a young spendthrift who loves Angelica, a witty heiress. His father schemes to disinherit him, while a crew of fops, sailors, and fortune-hunters plot around them. The play's talk is fast and polished, and its intrigues end in weddings.

Angelica's wit matches any man's, and the play's famous lines still sparkle. Congreve wrote it at the height of Restoration comedy. The play remains a favorite of actors for its dialogue, and it gives a lively picture of London love and money. The comedy's wit and sparkle still delight Restoration fans.
1412-masterman-ready:
Captain Frederick Marryat tells a Robinson Crusoe tale for young readers, in which the Seagrave family is wrecked on a Pacific island. Masterman Ready, an old seaman, guides them through building, farming, and defence. Marryat, a naval captain turned novelist, wrote for boys who loved the sea.

Ready's practical skill and quiet courage carry the family through storms, savages, and hardship, until rescue comes. Marryat writes from his own naval life, and the book became a favourite of Victorian boys. Ready, the old seaman, teaches the family to build, plant, and defend their island home.
1622-the-law-and-the-lady:
Wilkie Collins's Law and the Lady, subtitled in its first part Paradise Lost, follows a bride who discovers on her wedding journey that her husband was tried for murdering his first wife. The bride's mistake becomes a quest: she sets out to clear his name, or to learn the worst, with law books and determination.

Through a Scottish trial, a madhouse, and a villain's confession, Collins turns a wife into a detective. The novel's note to the reader warns that fiction's people act as real people do. It is a gripping Collins mystery, and an early tale of a woman investigating her own marriage.
1835-the-case-of-the-pool-of-blood-in-th:
Grace Isabel Colbron and Augusta Groner's Joseph Muller mystery opens in a village pastor's study, where a pool of blood waits for an explanation and no body to match it. Muller reasons that the criminal must live in or near the village, and therefore must be known to all and unlikely to excite suspicion, a rule the village doctor at once questions.

The inquiry moves through parish gossip, church business, and the small certainties of village life, with Muller testing each suspect against the blood in the study. The book is a village mystery of the classic kind. Its pleasure lies in watching a quiet detective use a community's own knowledge against a killer hiding inside it.
1913-the-drums-of-jeopardy:
Harold MacGrath's Drums of Jeopardy opens on a fast train into Albany on the New York Central from the West. It is three-thirty on a chill March morning in the first year of peace. A pall of fog lies over the world, and a stranger named Stefani Grazzi, with drums that beat a warning, draws a young woman named Kitty into danger.

The novel follows Kitty's questions — why hadn't the stranger been taken directly to the Roosevelt, and why all this pother and secrecy over a total stranger? The plot that follows runs through Russian exiles, stolen jewels, and revenge. MacGrath writes the postwar thriller with speed, and the drums themselves, beating through fog and city streets, give the book its pulse.
19719-the-art-of-writing-speaking-the-en:
Word Study forms one part of The Art of Writing and Speaking the English Language, dated 1903. Its lessons get down to single letters and sounds. One rule notes that long vowels before single consonant sounds end in silent e. Short vowels, the book points out, take no silent e. Rules like these fill its pages.

Self-improvement guides sold strongly in that era. Clerks, teachers, and new speakers wanted correct English fast. This volume teaches by list, rule, and example. It treats spelling as a system that can be mastered. Modern readers may find some rules stiff. The book still shows how English teaching worked before usage guides softened. It is a window into classroom practice of 1903.
1991-old-friends-essays-in-epistolary-pa:
Andrew Lang's Old Friends, essays in epistolary parody, imagines letters between famous figures of literature and history, written in their own voices and styles. Lang, a scholar and a wit, plays the game with learning: the parodies work because he knows the originals from the inside.

The essays move through centuries and genres, with each letter catching its writer's mannerisms, obsessions, and blind spots. The book is a delight for readers who know their classics. A gentle introduction for those who do not, since Lang's affection for his subjects keeps the parody kind.
20229-stories-of-comedy:
Stories of Comedy gathers comic tales from noted humor writers of the past. One sailor meets a stranger inclined to treat him with high airs. The stranger takes the same high hand on nautical subjects in return. At last he bursts out with a salty, laughing curse at the talk.

Sea yarns and barroom tales thrive on just such comic clashes. Each story in the set aims for a laugh from character and voice. Dialect, bluster, and tall claims do much of the comic work. Readers get a handy shelf of older humor, rough edges and all.
20359-the-lovely-lady:
The Lovely Lady, from 1913, is a tale of a house bathed in summer light. Greenish gold sunlight slants on orchard grass under apple trees. Arched windows let in the scent of cluster roses at the fence. Evening clamor of birds rises from Bloombury wood nearby.

Such lush openings mark the work of Mary Johnston, a famed novelist then. A lovely lady at a story's heart draws love, loss, and longing near. Johnston wrote of Virginia and the South with a poet's eye. Readers get a lyrical tale where place and feeling blend as one.
20540-my-man-sandy:
My Man Sandy is a book of humorous tales in broad Scots about Sandy, a farm servant of endless confidence. His wife tells the stories, and her dry patience is half the fun. Sandy's schemes for improving the farm defy all common sense.

He would have grown his cabbages with the stocks under the ground, his wife says. Just so, she explains, they could get the fresh air about their roots. It is just his way, you see. She would not wonder to find Donald yoked in the potato cart with his head where his tail should be. The tales were newspaper favorites in Scotland.
2062-all-for-love-or-the-world-well-lost:
John Dryden retells the story of Antony and Cleopatra in blank verse, after Shakespeare and after the Restoration stage had reopened. Antony, torn between Rome and Egypt, gives up empire for love, and the play follows that choice to its end. Dryden wrote All for Love in 1677, as a deliberate rival to Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra.

Dryden keeps the focus tight on the lovers, Octavia, and Ventidius, letting rhetoric carry the tragedy. The play stands as a high point of Restoration drama, and as Dryden's most praised attempt at heroic tragedy. He kept to the classical unities, compressing the action into a single place and a short span of time.
208-daisy-miller-a-study:
Daisy Miller, a fresh American girl touring Europe, charms and shocks polite society. Henry James's Daisy Miller, in the 1879 book text, opens at Vevey on Lake Geneva, where Winterbourne meets Daisy and her mother. Her frank manners puzzle the American colony.

In Rome, Daisy walks with an Italian, Giovanelli, past midnight and past propriety. Winterbourne cannot decide whether she is innocent or reckless. Fever in the Colosseum ends the question tragically. The study made James famous and Daisy a byword for American innocence abroad. Daisy's name entered everyday speech as shorthand for a free American girl.
21224-the-dyeing-of-cotton-fabrics-a-pra:
Franklin Beech, a practical colourist and chemist, wrote this handbook in 1901. He aimed it at dyers and students who needed modern dyeing processes in a small, clear book. Forty-four engravings illustrate the work. He says plainly that he chose brevity over completeness, keeping only methods experience had proved reliable.

The first chapter treats the structure and chemistry of the cotton fibre: what alkalies, acids, and oxidising agents do to cellulose. Scouring and bleaching follow, then the dyeing processes themselves. Beech insists that good dyeing starts with knowing the fibre. The book served working dyers in the great Lancashire and Yorkshire mills of its day.
2137-rosamund-queen-of-the-lombards-a-tr:
Algernon Charles Swinburne writes a verse tragedy set in Verona in June 573, where Rosamund, queen of the Lombards, faces King Albovine, the warrior Almachildes, and the old counsellor Narsetes. Love, revenge, and power drive the plot. Swinburne took Rosamund's story from Lombard history, where revenge drives queens and kings.

Swinburne's blank verse is rich and musical, and the play turns on a queen caught between duty and desire. The tragedy shows Swinburne the dramatist, working in the shadow of Shakespeare and the Italian chronicles. Verona in 573, with its palace halls, gives the tragedy its dark, early medieval stage.
2195-the-master-of-mrs-chilvers-an-impro:
Jerome K. Jerome turns a London drawing room into a comic battleground in this three-act play. Mrs. Chilvers rules her household at Russell Square with strong opinions, and the arrival of a would-be master sets off a war of wit about who truly runs a marriage. The comedy is improbable by design, and Jerome plays that fact for laughs.

Arguments about husbands, wives, and housekeeping escalate into delightful absurdity, with each character sure of a victory that slips away. The dialogue is brisk and the situations pile up fast. Readers looking for light Edwardian stage comedy will enjoy its cheerful nonsense and sharp lines.
22202-aunt-rachel-a-rustic-sentimental-c:
David Christie Murray called Aunt Rachel a rustic sentimental comedy. Murray knew the English countryside and its speech from his own upbringing. In his preface he promises not to exaggerate. He has fallen short, he says, of the characters he had to deal with. He gives their talk as near their own form as he can achieve.

The comedy turns on Aunt Rachel and the village lives around her. Courtship, gossip, and money troubles move the plot in the Murray manner. Rustic dialogue carries much of the humour. Murray's country novels were steady sellers, and this slight, kindly piece shows the vein of rustic comedy he worked for decades.
22288-chinese-painters-a-critical-study:
Raphael Petrucci wrote Chinese Painters: A Critical Study to introduce Western readers to China's painting. Petrucci had a knowledge of the world's art, the introduction says, that few men in Europe rivalled. He was also a scientific engineer and a novelist, and his study reached English readers in translation soon after his early death.

The study moves through China's great masters and schools, from early masters to the literati painters. Petrucci treats brushwork, emptiness, and spirit as seriously as European critics treated oil and perspective. When it appeared, Chinese painting was still a curiosity in the West. Petrucci's book is an early, earnest attempt at understanding it whole.
2280-a-millionaire-of-rough-and-ready:
Bret Harte sets this novel in a California mining town where sudden wealth upends old ties. A Millionaire of Rough-and-Ready follows a man made rich by the mines as he tries to buy respectability, love, and a place among people who remember his humbler days. The town's rough democracy resists his gold at every turn.

Harte fills the story with miners, widows, and speculators, all bargaining over money and reputation. The comedy of new riches carries a serious point about what wealth cannot purchase. Readers get a lively California novel about fortune's limits.
2379-chastelard-a-tragedy:
Algernon Charles Swinburne's verse tragedy Chastelard dramatizes the love of the French poet Chastelard for Mary, Queen of Scots, and his execution for it. The play's cast includes the four Marys, Darnley, and Murray, with Swinburne's lush, musical verse carrying the doomed passion. Written in his youth, it shows his gift for lyric drama.

The tragedy is more poetry than stagecraft, and its power lies in its language and its doomed atmosphere. Swinburne's Mary is proud, sensual, and tragic. Readers of Victorian verse drama will find a rich early work.
2917-the-skin-game-a-tragi-comedy:
John Galsworthy's tragi-comedy The Skin Game pits Hillcrist, a country gentleman, against Hornblower, a man newly rich, over land and standing. Hillcrist's wife Amy, daughter Jill, and agent Dawker face Hornblower's sons Charles and Rolf, with Chloe, Charles's wife, caught between the families. The epigraph warns that who touches pitch shall be defiled.

The action runs from Hillcrist's study to an auction room a month later, where Chloe sits motionless, fanning herself with sale particulars, while Jill offers smelling salts. Both sides sink toward the methods they despise, and the ending leaves nobody clean. The play remains a sharp study of old money, new money, and the price of winning.
3325-locrine-a-tragedy:
Algernon Charles Swinburne writes this verse tragedy from Britain's legendary past. The 1887 Chatto and Windus edition dedicates the play to Alice Swinburne, with verses on love that comes and goes like wind or fire, with words and wings to speak and flee. A deeper love, the dedication says, has neither wings nor words so light.

Locrine, son of Brutus and first king of Locrine, gives the play its hero and its doom. Love, kingship, and divided Britain drive the tragedy, in Swinburne's rich, musical blank verse. Swinburne's ancient kings speak in modern poetry, and fate works through passion rather than through politics.
3602-cupid-s-understudy:
Edward Salisbury Field writes a comic romance about a young woman named Elizabeth. Her father is neither a coal baron like Mr Tudor Carstairs, nor a captain of industry, nor heir to whisky distillers. Because her father lacks such wealth, Elizabeth cannot simply sit with the Four Hundred. That fashionable set of New York society bars her, and the story follows her efforts to find love and place anyway.

Field writes with light satire about money, manners, and the social ladder. Mockingbirds sing and linnets nest in honeysuckle, but for Elizabeth the world has changed, and nothing is quite the same again. The book suits readers who enjoy gentle American comedy about class, courtship, and a heroine who wins by charm rather than fortune.
383-she-stoops-to-conquer-or-the-mistake:
Oliver Goldsmith's comedy of errors turns on a young man too shy with fine ladies and too bold with barmaids. Charles Marlow, sent to court Kate Hardcastle, mistakes her father's house for an inn and treats his hosts as servants. Kate, quick and game, plays along as a maid to win him on her own terms.

A night of mix-ups follows, with a stolen jewel case, a runaway elopement plot, and servants in on the jest. Goldsmith wrote the play to push back against soft, weeping comedy, and its brisk wit still lands. The piece endures as a bright stage classic, full of high spirits and good sense.
4255-a-yorkshire-tragedy:
Printed in C. F. Tucker Brooke's 1918 edition of the Shakespeare Apocrypha, this short play bears the subtitle Not So New as Lamentable and True. It is set at Calverly Hall in Yorkshire, where servants gossip about their absent young master while his wife waits at home, anxious and unhappy.

The play belongs to the domestic tragedies of the early seventeenth century, which staged recent crimes for a London audience rather than inventing kings and battles. Its interest lies in that closeness to reported fact: a household, a marriage, and a master whose return brings ruin, told in plain, urgent dialogue rather than courtly verse.
539-a-w-kinglake-a-biographical-and-lite:
W. Tuckwell studies Alexander William Kinglake, author of Eothen and the History of the Invasion of the Crimea, in this 1902 biography. Eleven years after Kinglake's death, Tuckwell gathers friends' memories of his voice, wit, sarcasm, and reserve, plus a critical view of his books. Early years, literary life, and Madame Novikoff fill the chapters.

Tuckwell writes with fond, judicious care, urging readers to see Kinglake as he lived, not merely as he wrote. The study serves as a rare portrait of a Victorian man of letters, at once shy, sharp, and grand in his histories.
5435-the-stillwater-tragedy:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich sets this novel in the small New England town of Stillwater, opening just before daybreak as birds stir over pine woods and a swamp. The town wakes slowly, with wrens and robins in its orchards, while something darker gathers beneath the quiet surface. Aldrich builds the story from that contrast between a peaceful place and a crime.

As the title promises, a tragedy unfolds among Stillwater's households, with suspicion, evidence, and old secrets coming into play. Aldrich, better known as a poet and editor, writes the mystery with careful local detail. Readers get a nineteenth-century American novel of crime and small-town life, told with restraint.
5798-the-beautiful-lady:
Booth Tarkington's The Beautiful Lady opens with a narrator painfully aware of himself at the center of the world, as a living advertisement for the least amusing ballet in Paris. To be the day's sensation of the boulevards, he suggests, requires an eccentricity he would rather not possess, and his blushes mark the comedy. From that stage-struck opening, the novel follows beauty, vanity, and love in Parisian society.

Readers get Tarkington's polished social comedy, where reputation is a performance and feeling hides behind wit. The novel favors character and dialogue over grand incident, letting embarrassment and admiration drive the plot. It suits readers who enjoy novels of manners, Paris settings, and a narrator whose self-consciousness is itself the joke.
6109-how-to-study-and-teaching-how-to-st:
F. M. McMurry, professor of elementary education at Teachers College, Columbia, writes on how to study and teaching how to study, dedicating the volume to his friend Orville T. Bright. Some seven or eight years earlier, the question of teaching children to study appeared on a hasty list of class topics.

On later examination McMurry found the problem surprisingly difficult, wide, and neglected by teachers. Since then, how adults should study and how children should be taught to study have been his chief hobby. His ideas come partly from reading, but largely from observation, experiment, and talk with students.
6517-the-grey-lady:
Henry Seton Merriman begins with two boys in a first-class carriage on a fast train, one of them fixed on a moment he cannot shake off. From that bright, tense start, the novel fans out into cards, deals, ships at sea, and a count whose past will not stay quiet. The chapter titles alone hint at risk, bluff, and a life lived close to the edge.

Across two books, the plot moves from fields and streets to voyages and fights, with loyalty and honor weighed at each turn. Merriman writes with a cool, brisk hand, letting talk and action carry the mood rather than long speeches. The Grey Lady is a tale of youth, chance, and the price paid for a bold game.
6559-assyrian-historiography-a-source-st:
Albert Ten Eyck Olmstead argues that no sound history of Assyria can be written until its sources are weighed one by one. His chapters move from early Assyrian writers through Tiglath-Pileser, Ashur-nasir-apal, Shalmaneser, Sargon, Sennacherib, and Ashur-bani-apal, then on to the Babylonian chronicle and Berossus. Annals, display texts, and edited copies each get a close look.

Olmstead shows how royal scribes shaped, cut, and reworked the record, so a modern reader must look past the praise to the facts. The study is dense but plain in aim: to sort true history from court story. It remains a useful guide for anyone who wants to know how Assyrian history was first written down.
6583-serious-hours-of-a-young-lady:
Charles Sainte-Foi, in a French work turned into English by Philaletes, sets out how a young lady may live her faith with grace. His preface holds that Christian women, like guardian angels, can guide the world unseen, and that a girl must learn her calling early. The book thus aims to teach duty, modesty, and kind sense, not mere polish.

Practical counsels follow in clear, elevated prose, on home, society, and the heart. The writer knows human nature well, and speaks with warmth rather than with scolding. Serious Hours of a Young Lady is a devout conduct book for girls of an earlier age, still clear in its aim today.
6740-don-garcia-of-navarre-or-the-jealou:
Molière's Don Garcia of Navarre stands apart from his comic hits, as its introductory notice stresses. The Palais-Royal had opened in January 1661 with The Love-Tiff and Sganarelle, and with the young Spanish queen newly arrived in France, a taste for Spanish drama seemed to revive. Molière tried a heroic comedy in that grand Spanish style.

Don Garcia, a jealous prince, loves, doubts, and rages in verse, with honor and passion at war. The play is high, serious, and less funny than Molière's usual fare, which may explain its cooler welcome. Don Garcia of Navarre is a fascinating, ambitious side step in Molière's career.
7487-count-alarcos-a-tragedy:
Benjamin Disraeli based this tragedy on a celebrated Spanish ballad, though he warns that no historical authority supports its events. He sets the play in the thirteenth century, when Castile had recently won supremacy in Spain and Burgos, its magnificent capital, was building its famous cathedral. That age of comparative refinement, Disraeli argues, allows more complicated motives than the rude ballad could carry.

Count Alarcos, whose ancient house has long mingled with the narrator's fortunes, stands at the center of a tragedy of love, honor, and royal command. The king's will forces the count toward a dreadful choice between his wife and his duty, and the ballad's dark outcome follows. Disraeli's early tragedy shows the future prime minister already fascinated by power, passion, and the price of obedience.
7840-the-female-gamester-a-tragedy:
Gorges Edmond Howard's The Female Gamester, a tragedy, opens with Juvenal in Latin and English on avarice and dice, asking when purses, nay chests, were staked on a cast. Dedicated to the Countess of Charlemont and other ladies famed for virtue, it warns that rank sets an example for all.

Howard argues in a preface that he holds one view throughout: gaming ruins women, families, and society alike. The play that follows turns a woman's love of cards into tragic ruin, using the stage to preach against a fashionable vice that swept Georgian drawing rooms.
8439-games-for-everybody:
May C. Hofmann wrote Games for Everybody for hosts who feared a dull evening. Her foreword notes that a party can fail when guests do not mix or the hostess has planned no games. The book supplies what is needed for a pleasant home gathering, church social, or similar occasion. Games for all ages and group sizes fill its pages.

The book belongs to the age of parlor games, before radio and television changed home evenings, and it shows how hosts once planned fun by hand. Readers planning a retro party, or studying social life, will find ready-to-use games and a picture of sociability in an earlier America. It is practical first, and charming second.
8944-the-elect-lady:
George MacDonald writes The Elect Lady as a duplex edition, opening in a slate-flagged kitchen of moderate size, humble yet not quite a farmhouse kitchen. Utensils hinting at more artificial necessities than a farm usually grows. At a corner of a white deal table sit two young people, evidently different in rank, meeting on no level of friendship. The young woman, about four- or five-and-twenty, well grown and not ungraceful, dark-haired with dark hazel eyes and rather large. Handsome features full of intelligence, holds a paper that seems the subject of their talk.

Landlord's daughter and tenant's son, the first chapter's title, names the social gap the novel explores, through love, duty, and faith. MacDonald's late fiction treats class and conscience with quiet intensity.
a-millionaire-of-rough-and-ready:
Bret Harte begins with a prospector's dream come true: a piece of brown-stained quartz shot through with yellow metal, heavy in the hand. The finder, dazed by his luck, wanders off from his claim at Rough-and-Ready rather than shout the news. His strange behavior sets the camp talking.

Six chapters and a prologue follow what sudden gold does to the man and to the mining camp around him. Old debts, old friendships, and new temptations all rearrange themselves around the strike. Harte, who knew the California camps from their first fame, writes with dry humor about money's power to unmake a man's judgment. The tale is short and neatly turned.
a-w-kinglake-a-biographical-and-literary:
William Tuckwell wrote this biography and critical study of Alexander William Kinglake, published in London in 1902 as the title page records, eleven years after Kinglake's death. Tuckwell complains that so marked a contemporary had not yet been memorialized, and that a few more years would make the personal side of him unrecoverable. He sets out to recover the man as friends knew him.

Kinglake was famous for Eothen, his Eastern travel book, and for his huge history of the Crimean War. Tuckwell traces his training, his political and public life, and his conversation — the wit, sarcasm, and reserve that made him a fixture of the Athenaeum and of Holland House. The study mixes critical summary of the writings with social portrait, aiming to re-clothe its subject in his habit as he lived.
a-yorkshire-tragedy:
A Yorkshire Tragedy, printed in Tucker Brooke's Shakespeare Apocrypha from the 1918 Oxford edition, is a short domestic tragedy of a husband's ruin. The cast gives the design: Husband, Wife, a college master, a justice of the peace, and serving-men Oliver, Ralph, and Samuel. At Calverley Hall the servants gossip about their young mistress, pining in her husband's long absence in London. The Husband has gambled away his estate and his reason at the dice and the bottle. He comes home to a ruined house.

What follows is brutally short: debts, madness, and the murder of his own children. The play was printed in 1608 as Shakespeare's and is now usually given to Thomas Middleton. It draws on the real Calverley murders of 1605. Readers get the apocryphal canon at its darkest, ten scenes of a gentleman's fall with no gods and no comfort.
all-for-love-or-the-world-well-lost-a-tr:
John Dryden rewrites the Antony and Cleopatra story as a tight tragedy of five acts, each act holding a single scene in this text. The introductory note places Dryden, who lived from 1631 to 1700, at the head of Restoration letters. His Antony is no longer Shakespeare's world-ranging figure but a man narrowed to one love and one doom.

The play stays in Alexandria, at the temple of Isis and the palace, where Antony, Cleopatra, and the loyal Ventidius argue love against honor. Octavia's arrival raises the stakes before the fall. Dryden wrote in smooth blank verse and called this his favorite among his plays. Its clear design made it the standard Antony for a century.
assyrian-historiography-a-source-study:
Albert Ten Eyck Olmstead's Assyrian Historiography is a source study of how the ancient Assyrians wrote their own history. Published as a University of Missouri study, it argues that Assyrian history cannot be written well until its documents have been sorted, dated and weighed.

Olmstead moves from the earliest annals through Tiglath-Pileser the First, Ashur-nasir-apal, Shalmaneser the Third, Sargon, Sennacherib, Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal, separating royal annals from display inscriptions and later chronicles. A closing chapter treats the Babylonian Chronicle and Berossus, the later writer who retold Mesopotamian history for Greek readers. The book suits students of ancient history who want to know what the sources are before trusting the stories built on them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-of-our-:
Christians have honoured the Mother of God with special veneration from the start. Theology calls it hyperdulia, to set her honour apart from that given to other saints. It is no surprise, then, that after the main altar the most prominent altar is the one dedicated with special honour to the Mother of God. To mark this preference it usually stands in the church's most prominent position, at the right, or gospel, side of the main altar.

In general the name means any altar whose titular is the Blessed Virgin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anthony-maria:
Anthony Maria Anderledy, General of the Society of Jesus, born Berisal 1819, died Fiesole 1892. He entered the Society at Brieg in 1839, then taught classics at Freiburg. When the Jesuits were expelled from Switzerland in 1848, Anderledy came to America with fifty others. He was sent to St. Louis, ordained there in 1848 by Archbishop Kenrick. He was pastor of the German congregation at Green Bay for two years. He was recalled to Germany in 1850 to a missionary band.

He continued his studies until 1859, when he became German Provincial. During his six-year term he purchased Maria-Laach abbey. In 1865 he went to Maria-Laach as moral theology professor. In 1870 he was called to Rome as Assistant-General for German provinces. In 1883 Rome delegates elected him Vicar-General with succession rights to Father Beckx. On Beckx's death in 1887, he became General. He edited Reuter's Neo-Confessarius anew, enriched with valuable notes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-burgundy:
Burgundy takes its name from a Germanic tribe, the Burgundi, who took the fertile basins of the Rhone, Saone, and Loire from the Romans in the fifth century. They lost that first kingdom to the Franks in 534. The land won independence again in the late ninth century as two kingdoms, Transjurane and Cisjurane Burgundy, joined under Rudolf II in 935.

Imperial rule followed in 1038, when Conrad II won the crown for his son Henry III, and French sway grew over the next centuries. Lyons passed to France in 1310, and on the death of Charles the Bold in 1477 Louis XI took the duchy into France. The house of Burgundy later held wide states under Philip the Good and Charles the Bold, and Mary granted the Great Privilege to her subjects.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-the-:
The Patronage of Our Lady thanks Mary for victories over Saracens, heretics, and foes. Spain first received it in 1679 for all the provinces of Spain. Its Office comes from the Common of the Blessed Virgin. The Mass is the ancient Salve sancta parens of Mary.

Benedict XII ordered it in the Papal States for the third Sunday of November. Elsewhere the ordinary names some Sunday in November for its keeping. Many places add titles like Queen of All Saints and Mother of Graces to the feast. Ruthenians keep a kindred Pokrov feast of protection on 1 October.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-kennedy:
Bishop of St Andrews James Kennedy was born about 1406. He died on 10 May 1466. He came from the ancient Kennedy house of Dunure. He was son of Lady Mary, daughter of King Robert III, and thus cousin of the reigning James II. After studying on the Continent, he became bishop of Dunkeld in 1438 and abbot of Scone soon after, succeeding Henry Wardlaw as bishop of St Andrews in 1440.

Appointed chancellor in 1444, he vigorously reformed civil and church abuses rampant in Scotland, a reforming zeal that earned him enmity from many nobles. He soon resigned the chancellorship, finding it incompatible with church duties, to which he gave himself with great assiduity. Love of learning showed in his 1450 foundation of St Salvator's College, St Andrews, endowed munificently with approval from Nicholas V and Pius II, a reforming bishop-prince of fifteenth-century Scotland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-janos-hunyady:
János Hunyady was governor of Hungary, born about 1400 and dead on 11 August 1456. He was the heroic defender of Catholic faith against Ottoman advance and father of King Matthias I Corvinus. His family's origin and parentage were not settled until recently, when modern research cleared up many legends surrounding the Hunyadi house. Historian Bonfini derived the family from Rome's Corvina gens to flatter King Matthias.

Gáspár Heltai's chronicle made Hunyady the illegitimate son of King Sigismund and a Wallachian peasant girl. Others argued for purely Hungarian, Serb, or Wallachian origin. In light of modern research, the family may be taken as proven Rumanian in origin. János himself, however, may be regarded as Hungarian by birthplace, probably born in Transylvania. The entry presents a frontier captain whose legend outran his lineage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kandy:
Kandy was a diocese of Ceylon, cut from the Vicariate of Southern Colombo in 1883 and erected as a diocese on 1 September 1886. Suffragan of Colombo, it covered the Central and Uva provinces, where tea and rubber were the main industries. Its only vicar and first bishop was Dom Clement Pagnani, a Sylvestrine Benedictine born at Fabriano in 1834 and consecrated in 1879. The town of Kandy stood 1,734 feet above the sea, seventy-five miles by rail from Colombo, with 26,522 people in 1901.

Kandy had been the island's capital since 1592, and its kings ruled there until the last, Vikrama Raja Sinha, was taken by the British in 1815. The fourteenth-century Temple of the Tooth still drew annual festivities for Buddha's relic, brought to Ceylon about 311. The Portuguese had carried the tooth itself to Goa in 1560 and burned it publicly, though Buddhists disputed this and displayed a piece of ivory in proof of their claim.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kisfaludy:
Sandor Kisfaludy (1772-1844) and his brother Karoly (1788-1830) were Hungarian writers, one a lyric poet, the other a founder of Hungarian romantic letters. Sandor studied philosophy and law at Presburg, then joined the army and the Hungarian lifeguards in Vienna in 1792.

Posted to Milan, he was taken prisoner to Provence in 1796, freed the same year, fought in the Rhine campaign of 1799, and in 1800 married Rosa Szegedy, his early love. His Himfy love songs of 1801 and 1807, written in sonnet form under Petrarch's influence yet no servile copy, won him wide fame. Karoly, raised by a sister after his mother's death in childbirth, left Raab unfinished for the army and pioneered the Hungarian novel and romantic comedy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-little-office:
The Little Office of Our Lady is a short daily devotion to Mary, shaped to mirror the Church's Divine Office yet prayed in addition to it. Traces appear at Monte Cassino in the eighth century, and an office in her honour is tied to Ildephonsus in the seventh, with an Eastern office linked to John Damascene around 730.

Wide use came later, likely in the tenth century, helped by English devotion under Dunstan and Ethelwold. By the eleventh century secular clergy in Italy and France said it daily, and Peter Damian spread its choir use in Italian monasteries. Later sections follow its text, its feasts, and the orders that kept it or let it go.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lombardy:
Lombardy takes its name from the Longobards, the Germanic people who ruled much of Italy in the early Middle Ages. At their peak their land covered the north, much of the centre, and nearly all the south, save mountainous Calabria and a coastal strip holding Naples, Gaeta, and Amalfi.

Thirty-six duchies split the realm, from Pavia and Milan to Benevento and Spoleto. Frankish conquest, new states like Venice and Piedmont, and the Papal States shrank the name step by step. By modern times it meant the Milan region alone, bounded by Switzerland, the Ticino, the Po, and Lake Garda, a rich plain of cities and farms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-normandy:
Normandy, the old French province that became five departments in 1790, took its name from Danish and Norwegian raiders turned settlers. In Gallo-Roman times the land formed the second Lyonnaise province, then passed to Neustria under the Merovingians before Northmen began raiding in the ninth century.

Charles the Bald's gifts of land to some raiders backfired, yet conversion opened a new path, and Rollo's settlement grew into a duchy that shaped France and England. The entry follows its bishops, abbeys, and wars from Viking landings to the Norman age. Five departments formed from the province in 1790: Seine-Inférieure, Eure, Calvados, Orne, and Manche.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syriac-hymnod:
Syriac hymnody means the hymns, called madrashe, as opposed to poetical homilies, called mimre, which belong to narrative poetry. This entry adds their structure and liturgical use to the general article on hymnology. Syriac metre rests on a fixed count of syllables per verse, without distinguishing long and short, and verses run from two to twelve syllables.

Favourites are twelve-syllable verses in three measures of four. Seven-syllable verses use measures of four and three, and five-syllable verses use measures of two and three. Strophes group such verses and usually keep one construction throughout. Before the ninth century, acrostics were the only further artifice. These alphabetic patterns came from Psalms and Lamentations, sometimes marking each verse and sometimes each strophe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-cassi:
William Cassidy was an Albany journalist and editor whose pen shaped New York Democratic politics for a generation. Born at Albany in 1815, he died there in 1873. He studied at Albany Academy and Union College, graduating in 1833, read law with John Van Buren, served as state librarian from 1843, and edited the Albany Atlas. When the Atlas merged with the Argus, he led the combined paper until his death.

As a writer he was terse, sharp, vigorous, and learned, and in talk he had rare power. He sat in the state constitutional convention of 1871 and joined the 1872 commission to revise the constitution. His funeral at Albany's Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception drew Bishop McNeirny, and both houses of the legislature, then in session, adjourned in respect for the dead editor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-mazie:
William Maziere Brady was an Irish church writer who crossed from Anglican vicar to Catholic scholar of Vatican archives. Born at Dublin in 1825, he died at Rome in 1894. Nephew of Ireland's lord chancellor, he entered Trinity College, Dublin, in 1842 and took degrees through a doctorate in 1863. He served as Anglican curate and rector in Ireland, besides acting as chaplain to successive viceroys. His three-volume Clerical and Parochial Records of Cork, Cloyne and Ross of 1863 mined diocesan registers and libraries.

Brady campaigned in print for disestablishing the Irish Protestant Church, notably in Facts or Fiction of 1866, which ran to five editions and denied that Irish bishops had converted at Elizabeth's accession. After the Disestablishment Act passed, he worked in the Vatican archives on English, Irish, and Scottish church affairs, gave up his benefices, and entered the Catholic Church in May 1873. His archive work then fed two volumes on episcopal succession.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-the-c:
William the Clerk of Normandy was a thirteenth-century French poet whose bestiary and allegories survive in part. Nothing is known of his life beyond his clerkship in Normandy. Works assigned to him with fair certainty include the Bestiaire Divin, a moral and theological treatise on man and beasts, likely from about 1210. Its dove passage laments the Church in England in 1208. The Besant de Dieu, an allegorical poem of 1226, Joies Nostre Dame, and a Life of Tobias complete the list.

A legend of Saint Magdalen is also credited to him. The Roman de Tergus, the fabliaux Prestre et Alison, Male Honte, and La Fille à la Bourgeoise are no longer counted his. Though he may have lived a time in England, as many Norman clerks did, he wrote in French, not Anglo-Norman dialect. His bestiary and allegories offer a window on medieval moral teaching drawn from nature.
chastelard-a-tragedy:
Algernon Charles Swinburne wrote Chastelard as a verse tragedy on Mary Queen of Scots and the French poet who loved her to death. Swinburne dedicates the play to Victor Hugo, calling him the chief of living poets. The scene is Holyrood, where Mary Stuart's four Maries sing and tease one another about lovers while Pierre de Chastelard watches, already lost.

Chastelard, caught hiding in the queen's chamber, faces execution rather than deny his love, and the tragedy moves through court intrigue with Darnley, Murray, and Morton in attendance. Swinburne pours his gift for music into the blank verse; song opens the play and rhythm carries its doom. It is the first panel of his Mary Stuart trilogy, lush, fatal, and unmistakably his.
count-alarcos-a-tragedy:
Benjamin Disraeli's Count Alarcos is a tragedy founded on a celebrated Spanish ballad, for whose events Disraeli admits no historical authority exists. He therefore fixes the action in the thirteenth century, when Castile had lately gained supremacy in Spain and Burgos, its magnificent capital, was building its famous cathedral.

That comparative refinement, Disraeli argues, permits more complicated motives than the rude ballad allowed, while Castilian factions, strong passions, enormous crimes and profound superstition still flourish. The dramatis personae include the King of Castile, Count Alarcos, the Count of Sidonia, the Prior of Burgos, and Oran the Moor. Readers of Disraeli's early work will find Alarcos romantic, stately and ambitious.
cupid-s-understudy:
Edward Salisbury Field spun a light society romance in Cupid's Understudy, told by a rich girl who knows her standing is shaky. Elizabeth Middleton narrates how her father Tom rose from keeping a livery stable in San Bernardino, California. A lucky mining venture with three burros and a Swedish prospector made him seven million dollars. Society still whispers about the stable over cocktails.

Field sets the tale among wealthy visitors in southern California, where old families guard every drawing room door. Elizabeth watches climbers, snobs, and suitors while her warm-hearted father blunders through polite rules. A love plot grows inside the comedy of manners, with class pride as the main obstacle. Dialogue stays quick and the satire stays gentle rather than bitter. Readers who enjoy early American high-society comedy, told in a bright first-person voice, will settle into this one fast.
daisy-miller-a-study:
Henry James wrote Daisy Miller: A Study, published in 1878, the tale that first carried his name across the Atlantic. Daisy Miller is a young American from Schenectady, traveling in Europe with her mother and small brother. At Vevey in Switzerland she meets Winterbourne, an American long settled abroad. He is drawn to her freshness and puzzled by her free manners.

In Rome, Daisy walks out with Giovanelli, an Italian of no standing, and the American colony cuts her for it. Winterbourne wavers between defending her innocence and judging her lost. A night visit to the Colosseum gives her Roman fever, and she dies still claiming she was never engaged. James turns a small scandal into a lasting study of innocence, custom, and judgment.
demosthenes-olynthiacs-philippics-kenned:
Demosthenes, the greatest orator of Athens, delivered the Olynthiacs and Philippics around 350 BC to wake his city to danger. Charles Rann Kennedy's English translation is the text here. King Philip of Macedon was swallowing Greek cities one by one, and Athens was drifting.

The Olynthiacs urge Athens to send real help to Olynthus, the city Philip was besieging, and to pay for it from the festival fund. The Philippics go further, naming Philip an enemy of all Greek freedom and calling for a standing defense. Athens acted too late; Olynthus fell, and Philip won Greece in the end. The speeches remain the peak of Greek political oratory.
