don-garcia-of-navarre-or-the-jealous-pri:
Molière's Don Garcia of Navarre, or The Jealous Prince, is a heroic comedy in five acts, presented here in English with the original French text alongside. The play was first brought out in Paris on 4 February 1661. A taste for Spanish drama had lately revived, and a Spanish company was performing Lope de Vega and Calderon in the city.

Don Garcia's jealousy drives the plot, as heroic love, honour and misunderstanding collide in the high Spanish manner Molière was trying for the occasion. The introductory notice stresses how unlike the play is to Molière's lighter comedies of the same season, such as The Pretentious Young Ladies. Readers and students of French classical theatre will find it an instructive curiosity: Molière reaching beyond comedy toward romance, and not quite succeeding.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PlotkinJudy_Plo:
Harold Weisberg wrote this letter on October 7, 1978, to a correspondent he calls Sandy. He writes about his freedom-of-information work, the slow extraction of records from agencies. He mentions an index of records received, the researcher's ledger of what had arrived. He also reports on his New Orleans investigations.

By 1978, Weisberg's FOIA suits were his main weapon, and an index was how he kept thousands of pages usable. The letter shows the bookkeeping behind the headlines: requests filed, pages logged, leads in New Orleans still being worked fifteen years after the assassination. It is a status report from inside a one-man archive, sent to a friend in the same struggle.
how-to-study-and-teaching-how-to-study:
How to Study and Teaching How to Study, by Frank M McMurry, professor of elementary education in Teachers College, Columbia University, treats studying itself as a skill to be taught. McMurry's preface tells how the question reached him, almost by accident, in a list of topics prepared for one of his classes. Examining it, he was surprised both by its difficulty and by how completely teachers had neglected it, and it became his chief hobby for years.

Two questions structure the book. How should adults study? How should children be taught to study? Three parts develop his answers from observation, experiment, and discussion with his students, whose contributions he expects them to recognize in the text. Against the school habit of assigning lessons and hoping, McMurry argues for purpose. Questions should be formed in advance. Method should be supervised. The volume helped found the study skills movement in American education.
inspector-french-and-the-starvel-tragedy: Inspector French and the Starvel Tragedy, Freeman Wills Crofts's mystery. The Starvel case. This book preserves that detective tale. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
judy:
Judy is a novel by Temple Bailey, copyrighted in 1907 by Little, Brown and Company. Bailey dedicates the book to her father. Twenty-seven chapters follow Judy through one summer, from The Judge and Judy to The Summer Ends. Anne, Tommy Tolliver, Launcelot, and Perkins the servant move through the chapter titles.

Episodes include a rain and a runaway, a white Sunday and a blue Monday, and a fortune and a fright. Spanish coins, a precious pussy cat, and castaways in a silver boat add storybook color. Judy keeps a promise, plays Lady Bountiful, and Anne hears a burglar. Bailey writes a bright, gentle tale of a girl's summer among family and friends.
locrine-a-tragedy:
Algernon Charles Swinburne published this tragedy with Chatto and Windus in 1887. Spottiswoode printed the London edition at New Square. Swinburne reserves the right of translation on the title page. He dedicates the play to Alice Swinburne in verse.

The dedication argues no words can utter deep love. Love stands clearer than the unsounded sea, he writes. Time and death are less than love, the poem insists. His Locrine retells the same British legend in passionate verse. False, the dedication cries, when man deems life more than breath. Sovereign song cannot lift such love homeward, Swinburne argues.
love-for-love-a-comedy:
Love for Love is a comedy by William Congreve, the Restoration playwright. This text follows the 1895 Methuen edition of his comedies. Congreve dedicated the play to the Earl of Dorset, a great patron of poets. Its Latin motto warns of a young man ready to play the madman.

Valentine, the hero, is deep in debt and in love with Angelica. He feigns madness to escape his father's hard bargain. Angelica, rich and witty, tests whether his love is real. Servants, sailors, and fortune-tellers crowd the comic scenes. The dialogue sparkles with some of the best wit in English comedy. The play made the young Congreve's name in 1695.
love-s-comedy:
Love's Comedy is an early play by Henrik Ibsen, in C. H. Herford's translation. Ibsen published it at Christiania in 1862, and polite society was indignant. The introduction here tells how the play mocked the trivial ways of the respectable. It even dared to bring a clergyman onto the stage.

The verse comedy follows young lovers and the talk that surrounds them. Ibsen asks whether love can live inside dull, safe marriage. His lovers fear that habit and comfort will kill true feeling. The writing is lighter than his later famous plays. Still, the sting of his social criticism is already plain to see.
magic-a-fantastic-comedy:
Magic is a fantastic comedy by G. K. Chesterton, published by Putnam in 1913. It was first staged at the Little Theatre, London, that November. The whole action passes in a duke's drawing room. The cast joins a doctor, a clergyman, and a duke's secretary.

At the center stands a Stranger and young Patricia Carleon. The Stranger is a conjurer whose tricks may be more than tricks. His magic forces the room to argue about faith and fact. Doctor Grimthorpe and the Reverend Cyril Smith take opposing sides. Chesterton turns a stage trick into a bright debate. The play glitters with his paradox and good humor.
masterman-ready: Captain Marryat wrote Masterman Ready, and Project Gutenberg lists it as the first in its Marryat set, dated August 1998. The hosted sample for this entry preserves only the file header and license notes. No readable page of the tale itself appears in the sample. For that reason this note stays with the title, the author, and the source. The content of the book cannot be described from the sample held here.
my-little-lady:
Eleanor Frances Poynter published this novel in 1871, her first book. Tauchnitz issued it in two volumes for British readers abroad. The Saturday Review praised its heroine as fresh and natural. It compared her to a Greuze head, innocent yet arch.

The review called the whole book charming and quietly told. Character and story both held its interest, the critic said. Poynter went on to write Ersilia and Among the Hills. She also translated German tales for English readers. This first novel was even turned into French as Madeleine Linders, a sign of its early charm.
nasa-tm-19650010243-imp-d-e-feasibility-:
Paul G Marcotte at Goddard Space Flight Center prepared this January 1964 feasibility study. It asks whether Interplanetary Monitoring Platform spacecraft, called IMP D and IMP E, could be placed in orbit around the Moon. The craft would weigh about one hundred eighty-one pounds.

Marcotte reports that the plan could work. A thrust-augmented Delta rocket with an extra third stage and a retrorocket could do the job. In the improved case, the chance of a stable lunar orbit was better than ninety percent. The study gave planners a concrete option, with odds stated plainly.
nasa-tm-19670019469-optimal-computing-fo:
C. R. Herron, E. R. Lancaster, and W. R. Trebilcock, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this computing paper in May 1967. It seeks the best computing forms for the C and S series of the two-body problem. Those equations govern two bodies moving under their shared gravity.

Classical solutions split into three cases, elliptic, parabolic, and hyperbolic, each with different mathematics. A unified treatment covering all three becomes possible by introducing the special C and S functions. Direct series for those functions converge for every input, but slowly when the input grows large. The authors present approximations for the functions and their derivatives that cut computing time sharply compared with plain Taylor series. Reduction formulas handle the large-input range, so one formulation serves every orbit type.
nasa-tm-19720008557-laminarization-model:
James F Schmidt, Donald R Boldman, and Carroll Todd of the Lewis Research Center presented this flow model in February 1972, as NASA TM X-2501. In a rocket nozzle, the boundary layer speeds up so hard that turbulence can partly die out. That shift is called laminarization. It changes friction and heating on the nozzle wall. Predicting it well matters for nozzle design and cooling.

Their model splits the layer into two regions. Near the wall sits a fully smooth sublayer. Above it rides a turbulent wake region that still mixes. They placed the model inside a step by step boundary layer calculation. An errata sheet later corrected the key of one figure. The model aimed to match real nozzle flows better.
old-friends-essays-in-epistolary-parody:
Andrew Lang published these playful essays in London in 1890. The full title calls them essays in epistolary parody. Most pieces first appeared in the St. James's Gazette. Lang invents letters by famous writers and characters. He added notes, an opening essay, and two letters here.

His parodies bite gently, so the victims smiled. Readers who know Dickens and other authors gain most. Lang drops two pieces by another friendly hand. The book offers light, bookish fun from a master critic. Lang's own voice stays light, learned, and full of private jokes.
phrases-for-public-speakers-and-paragrap:
Grenville Kleiser compiled Phrases for Public Speakers and Paragraphs for Study in 1910, and his address to the student sets out the method. Experienced speakers, he says, acquire hundreds of phrases they use over and over, since stock phrases hold a thought together and allow fluent speech on short notice. The book is one of practise, not theory.

Students should read several pages aloud daily, think what each phrase means, and fill it out in their own words. The second part reprints paragraphs from notable speeches so students can study climax and other effects. A month of earnest practise, Kleiser promises, yields astonishing results.
podcast-dannyjones-gYP6Ira1adY:
Filmmaker Randall Nickerson joins Danny Jones to argue that alien abduction still goes on today. Nickerson is known for a film on a famous mass sighting by school children in Zimbabwe. He now works with people who report new cases.

Nickerson shares fresh reports and the toll they take on the people who live them. He argues the pattern matches the old cases too well to be a fad. Jones asks how he sorts true tales from false ones. Listeners get a sober take on a topic most media treats as a joke. The library keeps the talk as an archive record.
podcast-tuckercarlson--L9Y3ht1tDY:
Political assassinations and the war involving Iran and Israel anchor this Tucker Carlson episode. Carlson connects killings of leaders, a surprise player in the Iran conflict, and Israel's latest bombing campaign. He presents the pieces as one grim picture of a world sliding toward wider war.

The host works through each event and asks who gains from the chaos. He questions official accounts and the roles of intelligence services in the shadows. Viewers get his running theory of a coordinated push toward conflict. The watching and the worried receive a dark briefing for a dark stretch of news.
ravenna-a-study: Ravenna: A Study, by Edward Hutton, with pictures by Harald Sund, is dated 1913 and dedicated to Arthur Symons. Only the contents are shown. The chapters run in order. They start with Ravenna's geographical and political position. Julius Caesar and the Empire follow. Honorius and Galla Placidia come next. Then come the fall of the West and Theodoric. The reconquest under Belisarius follows. The Lombard invasion and the Papal State lead to the churches. Catholic, Arian, and Byzantine churches are treated. S. Vitale and S. Apollinare in Classe close the list.
rosamund-queen-of-the-lombards-a-tragedy: Algernon Charles Swinburne wrote Rosamund, Queen of the Lombards, a tragedy printed in London in 1899 by Chatto and Windus. The cast lists Albovine, king of the Lombards, the young warrior Almachildes, and the old leader Narsetes, with Rosamund as queen and Hildegard as a noble maiden. The scene is Verona, and the time is June 573. Act I opens in a hall in the palace, with a curtain drawn across it, as Albovine and Narsetes enter.
sandy: Alice Hegan Rice, author of Mrs. Wiggs of the Cabbage Patch, wrote Sandy, issued in New York in 1905 by the Century Company. Rice gives the book to her aunt, Miss Mary A. Hegan, who used to tell her better stories than she shall ever write. A front picture shows Sandy looking up at a slender little girl in a long tan coat and a white tam-o'-shanter.
science-in-arcady: Grant Allen wrote Science in Arcady, issued in London in 1892 by Lawrence and Bullen, and given to Grant Richards in grateful acknowledgment of many kind offices. An avuncular greeting heads the contents. The contents list fourteen essays, opening with My Islands, Tropical Education, and On the Wings of the Wind. Later titles include A Desert Fruit, Pretty Poll, High Life, Eight-Legged Friends, Mud, The Greenwood Tree, and Fish as Fathers.
serious-hours-of-a-young-lady:
Charles Sainte Foi wrote this French guide for young women, here in English by a translator signing as Philaletes. A preface praises the book's high views and deep knowledge of the human heart. It holds that women, like guardian angels, can guide the world unseen.

Sainte Foi sets out a young girl's duties and the role she will one day fill in home and society. Clear, delicate counsel fills the pages, aimed at forming faith and conduct. The preface claims the French original won a wide welcome and did lasting good, and it hopes the English version will serve the same end.
she-stoops-to-conquer-or-the-mistakes-of:
Oliver Goldsmith wrote this comedy of a night's mistakes and inscribed it to Samuel Johnson. Goldsmith thanks Johnson for backing a play that dared to shun mere sentiment. The piece reached the stage late in its season, yet won the public, he reports with relief.

David Garrick supplied a prologue that mourns the comic muse as dying. The play answers that gloom with brisk folly: a young man mistakes a great house for an inn and its daughter for a servant. Goldsmith's plot of errors still fills theatres, a high point of laughing comedy in English.
the-beautiful-lady:
Booth Tarkington's narrator begins in Paris, blushing at the centre of attention as a living advertisement for a dull ballet. All Paris, he says, laughs at him on the boulevards. Coachmen stand in their boxes, children are lifted to see him, and crowds block the pavement.

Yet he wears rich grey clothes and fine linen, carries no placard, and speaks to no one. For seven days he sits hatless at a small table under the awning of the Cafe de la Paix, drinking coffee morning and afternoon. His shame comes not from rags or labour, but from being stared at in silence for hours.
the-boss-of-little-arcady: Harry Leon Wilson wrote The Boss of Little Arcady, from 1905. The book is split in two parts, The Book of Colonel Potts and The Book of Miss Caroline. The first part's chapters start with how the Boss won his title and the golden day of Colonel Potts. The Perfect Lover, Dreams and Wakings, and A Mad Prank of the Gods come next. Billy Durgin as a sleuth crowds the mid parts. How the Boss saved himself and the uplift of Little Arcady close it.
the-bread-winners-a-social-study:
The Breadwinners: A Social Study came out in New York and London from Harper and Brothers in 1901. No author's name is printed on the pages shown. The first part is called A Morning Call. A French clock on the mantel, framed of brass and crystal, strikes ten with a slow clang like a far church bell. A gentleman reading a newspaper by the fire looks up to save himself the count.

The man is drawn with care: light gray eyes with a glint of steel, black hair, and a dark brown mustache. His clothes are of the spring style seen in the front windows of the Knickerbocker Club in the year 187-. His room fits him: dwarf bookcases of carved oak, books in soft browns and reds, and walls of Cordovan leather stamped with gold fleurs-de-lis.
the-brown-study: Grace S. Richmond wrote The Brown Study, dated 1919. Richmond had also written Red Pepper Burns and The Twenty-Fourth of June. She gave the book to the living memory of Edwards Park Cleaveland. Its chapters all hang on one man: Brown Himself, Brown's Caller, and Brown's Borrowed Baby. Brown's Sister Sue and Brown's Unborrowed Baby come next. Brown's Brown Study and Brown's New World close the list. No tale page is shown.
the-busie-body: Susanna Centlivre wrote The Busie Body, a play of 1709. This copy is number 19 of the Augustan Reprint Society issues, printed at Los Angeles by the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library of the University of California in 1949. An introduction by Jess Byrd stands at its head. The rest of the pages shown are lists of the society's editors. The general editors are H. Richard Archer, Richard C. Boys, Edward Niles Hooker, and H. T. Swedenberg, Jr. No page of the play itself is shown.
the-case-of-the-pool-of-blood-in-the-pas:
The Case of the Pool of Blood in the Pastor's Study, by Grace Isabel Colbron and Augusta Groner, is fronted by the series introduction to Joe Muller. He serves the Imperial Austrian police. He is one of the great experts of his profession. Yet he is a small, slight, plain-looking man. His chief characteristic is humbleness of mien.

That humility began with a miscarriage of justice in his early youth. It gave him several years in prison. A stigma then closed honest employment to him long after. The misfortune drove him into the police, and official red tape keeps his standing low even while kings and councillors consult him and his department prizes him. The introduction lingers on the man at length before the pastor's study and its pool of blood can claim him.
the-circular-study: Anna Katharine Green wrote this mystery, dated 1900, shown here in a 1914 Garden City edition from Doubleday, Page and Company. Only the title page and contents are present here. Book I, headed A Strange Crime, names a red light, a mute servitor, five small spangles, and Mr. Gryce facing a new experience. Book II is headed Remember Evelyn and opens with the secret of the Cadwaladers.Front matter alone is a thin basis, and it is all there is.
the-diary-of-a-nobody:
George Grossmith and Weedon Grossmith wrote The Diary of a Nobody, in a new edition printed at Bristol by J. W. Arrowsmith and sold in London by Simpkin, Marshall, Hamilton, Kent and Company, with illustrations by Weedon Grossmith. An introduction by Mr. Pooter asks why he should not publish his diary. He has often seen the reminiscences of people he never heard of, and sees no reason, just because he is not a Somebody, why his diary should not interest readers.

Chapter I settles Charles Pooter and his dear wife Carrie in their new house, The Laurels, Brickfield Terrace, Holloway. It is a nice six-roomed residence with a front breakfast-parlour, a little front garden, and ten steps up to a front door kept chained. Tradesmen trouble them a bit, and intimate friends like Cummings and Gowing come to the little side entrance.
the-double-dealer-a-comedy:
The Double-Dealer, a comedy taken from the 1895 Methuen edition, opens with a long dedication to Charles Montague of the Treasury. Its author owns the play's faults at once: he meant to write a true and regular comedy, found the task hard, and fell short in part. Yet he claims the build of the plot is regular, as a house built to a plan.

William Congreve's play of masks and plots follows. A smooth villain works on a young heir while seeming his friend. The dedication's candour about craft is itself a small essay on how plays get made.
the-drums-of-jeopardy:
Harold MacGrath's The Drums of Jeopardy opens on a fog-bound March dawn at Albany station, in the first year of peace after the Great War. A man in a long black coat, derby low, swings a scarred English kitbag and waits with his back to the wall till the platform clears. Close behind him pads a short, thick man of strange speed.

Sixteen thousand miles of flight lie behind the tall man, by horse, camel, ship, and train. Gems, Bolshevik agents, and a woman's honour drive this chase tale. MacGrath keeps the pace hot and the stakes rich.
the-elect-lady:
George MacDonald's The Elect Lady opens in a farm kitchen of slate flags, where two young folk sit across a white deal table. The woman, a landlord's daughter of some twenty-five years, holds a paper that rules their talk. She looks able and proud. The young man, a tenant's son, seems the weaker of the two and defers to her.

Rank and faith will test them both. MacDonald, a Scots minister turned novelist, writes of pride bowed by love and grace. The chapter head names their stations at once: landlord's daughter and tenant's son.
the-false-one-a-tragedy:
Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher wrote The False One, a tragedy set in Egypt in the days of Julius Caesar. The cast lists Caesar, King Ptolomy, Cleopatra and her sister Arsino, plus priests, captains, and turncoat Romans.

The play opens with Achillas and Achoreus, a priest of Isis, speaking of love for the king. Court plots turn on who shall rule Egypt and who shall win Caesar's ear. Cleopatra stands listed as Caesar's mistress, and her guard and waiting woman fill out her court. Ambition, lust, and war drive the action toward the famous deaths of that age.
the-female-gamester-a-tragedy: Gorges Edmond Howard wrote The Female Gamester as a tragedy on the vice of gaming. The title page spells the name Gamester. Only the front matter is present here. A verse motto from Juvenal tells of whole chests staked at the dice. A dedication praises three ladies for fine conduct. A note to the reader then takes up how English tragedy sets its scenes too high. No act or speech of the play appears in these opening pages.
the-gods-and-mr-perrin-a-tragi-comedy: Hugh Walpole wrote The Gods and Mr. Perrin. Its subtitle is A Tragi-Comedy. George H. Doran Company printed it in New York in 1911. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, a motto from Pilgrim's Progress, and a letter of dedication to Punch. The letter is dated Chelsea, January 1911. Walpole recalls a day in a French town. He first showed Punch the figure of Mr. Perrin there. The contents begin with Mr. Perrin drinking his tea.
the-grey-lady: Henry Seton Merriman wrote The Grey Lady. Its motto is: The dog that snapt the shadow, dropt the bone. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list in two books. Book the First has sixteen chapters. They open with Two in the Field and A Man Down. They name A Sea Dog, Purgatorio, and Don Quixote. Book the Second has fourteen chapters. They name For the Highest Bidder and A Great Fight. They end with The Count's Story. No chapter text is present.
the-jervaise-comedy:
J. D. Beresford published this novel with Macmillan in 1919. The contents trace a country-house weekend gone wrong. The first hour, Anne, and Frank Jervaise open it. Daybreak, morning, and notes and queries follow. The outcast, Banks, and the home farm come next. Conversion, Farmer Banks, and Mrs. Banks continue it. Remembrance and a postscript close the list. The postscript promises the true story.

Chapter I opens in a retrospective voice. The narrator recalls the thrill he actually felt. It came delightfully, yet blended with a threat of dismay. He savors that dramatic moment warmly. A rare adventure had arrived suddenly in ordinary life. Beresford builds his comedy on a dance and a disappearance. The Jervaise household interrogates itself through one night and morning. The Canadian Banks family gets drawn into its embarrassment.
the-law-and-the-lady:
Wilkie Collins addressed readers in a short note dated London, February 1, 1875, before his mystery novel begins. He asks them to recall that people do not always act by pure reason. Love, he warns, often falls on objects friends judge less deserving.

Part one, called Paradise Lost, opens at Valeria wedding. Her uncle Starkweather reads the marriage service while her aunt taps her shoulder and announces that she is married. Valeria feels bewildered, and her new husband looks nearly as lost. Collins starts a marriage plot with a bride mistake that hints at hidden trouble.
the-life-of-jesus-of-nazareth-a-study: Rush Rhees published his study of the life of Jesus of Nazareth with Scribner, copyrighted in 1900. Only the title page and the start of a detailed contents are present here, opening part one with the historical situation in nineteen sections. Those sections cover Herod the Great and his sons, Roman procurators, taxes, the army, Sadducees, Pharisees, Zealots, Essenes, and messianic hope. The study itself stays beyond the pages held in this record beyond that outline.
the-maids-tragedy: Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher's The Maid's Tragedy appears here with its list of persons and the first two lines of dialogue. The play does not appear beyond its opening. The persons include the King and his brother Lysippus. Amintor, a gentleman, and Evadne, Amintor's wife, follow. Her brothers Melantius and Diphilus come next, with Aspatia, troth-plight wife to Amintor. Her father Calianax, a humorous lord, completes the list. That pairing of a wife and a plighted bride around one man signals the tragedy's knot before the play begins.
the-master-of-mrs-chilvers-an-improbable: Jerome K. Jerome imagined The Master of Mrs. Chilvers, an improbable comedy published by T. Fisher Unwin in 1911. Only the title page, the outline of acts, and the start of the cast list are present here, so the play's dialogue does not appear. The four acts move from a Russell Square drawing room to a Liberal committee room, then to the town hall in East Poplar at ten at night. The final act returns to Russell Square at midnight.
the-old-bachelor-a-comedy:
William Congreve's comedy The Old Bachelor appears in the 1895 Methuen edition of his comedies, the first of four plays. A long introduction opens the volume. It takes up two charges often laid against old comedies: gross language and immorality, charges sharpened by Jeremy Collier's famous attack on the stage.

The introduction argues that grossness is a matter of time and place, since each age finds its own names for the same things. It also warns against expecting everything in every work. Readers get a defense of Restoration comedy before they reach Congreve's witty play about a bachelor who fears marriage.
the-photoplay-a-psychological-study:
Hugo Münsterberg wrote The Photoplay: A Psychological Study. D. Appleton and Company published it in New York and London in 1916. The contents split the book into two parts. The first treats the psychology of the photoplay: depth and movement, attention, memory and imagination, and emotions. The second treats its esthetics, on the purpose and means of art.

Chapter One asks where the growth of the moving pictures began. Was it the first device that put movement into pictures on a screen, or something earlier? Münsterberg, a psychologist, treats the young cinema as a serious art of the mind. His book is one of the first full studies of film as more than a novelty.
the-pretty-lady: Arnold Bennett's novel The Pretty Lady, dated 1918, opens with a motto from Samuel Butler. Butler holds that virtue has never been well represented by the virtuous, and that the sub-vicious understand it best. The pages shown give the title page, the motto, and the start of the contents. Early chapters are titled The Promenade, The Power, The Flat, and Confidence. Ostend, The Albany, For the Empire, and Boots follow. Later entries include The Club, The Mission, The Telegram, and Rendezvous. The story itself is not shown.
the-saint-s-tragedy:
A tragedy in verse opens with a list of characters headed by Elizabeth, daughter of the King of Hungary. Lewis, Landgrave of Thuringia, was betrothed to her in childhood. His brother Henry and several vassals appear. So does Conrad of Marpurg, a monk acting as the Pope's commissioner against heresy. No author is named in the pages shown.

The scene lies mainly in Eisenach and the Wartburg. It changes afterwards to Bamberg and finally to Marpurg. A proem in verse, spoken by Epimetheus, calls the Teutonic father-ages to wake again. It asks how saintly mothers schooled themselves by vigil, fast, and prayer. It also recalls crusading fathers who fought and died for God, not for gold.
the-scornful-lady:
A comedy called The Scornful Lady opens with a list of persons represented. Elder Loveless is a suitor to the Lady. Young Loveless is a prodigal. Savil serves as steward to the elder brother. The Lady and Martha are two sisters. Welford is another suitor, and Morecraft is an usurer. No author is named in the pages shown.

Act one begins with the two Lovelesses, Savil, and a page. Elder Loveless asks whether hope is past with Morecraft. The usurer holds Young Loveless's mortgage. Young Loveless replies that the hope is hopelessly past. Morecraft has sucked in ten thousand pounds worth of his land, he says. He paid less for it at a gulp. Elder Loveless answers that his own task is as hard. He must persuade a passionate woman, or leave the land.
the-skin-game-a-tragi-comedy: John Galsworthy's The Skin Game, a tragi-comedy dated 1920 in its header, belongs to his fourth series of plays. A series list precedes the title page. The fourth holds A Bit O'Love, The Foundations, and this play. An epigraph serves as the play's motto. Who touches pitch shall be defiled, it warns. The pages shown give the series list, title, and motto only. No cast list, scene setting, or dialogue follows in this record, so the play itself is not shown.
the-spanish-curate-a-comedy: A comedy of Spanish intrigue, presented here through its list of persons only. Don Henrique is described as an uxorious lord, cruel to his younger brother Don Jamie. The covetous lawyer Bartolus has a wife, Amaranta, whom the gentleman Leandro wantonly loves. Leandro's friends Angelo, Milanes, and Arsenio back him, so the play's dialogue does not appear in these pages.
the-stillwater-tragedy:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich sets this novel in the village of Stillwater. The scene opens close upon daybreak. A wall of pines and hemlocks holds off the west wind. Frogs twang from the swamp by the highway. Birds break into their wild morning chorus over orchards and gardens. Below them the village lies deathly still.

Perhaps nobody hears the music but the watchers at one bedside. Leonard Tappleton lies there. He is the town's richest man. He has been dying for three days. He cannot last until sunrise. Aldrich's dawn panorama moves past Slocum's marble yard, looking like a cemetery in embryo, and farm lanterns in barn-yards, building the stillness against which the tragedy will break.
the-three-additions-to-daniel-a-study: William Heaford Daubney, formerly vicar of Harlington and rector of Leasingham, published The Three Additions to Daniel at Cambridge in 1906. This record shows his title page and a dedication to his wife Alice. It also shows an analysis listing eight questions. They cover title and position, authorship, date and place, purpose, the state of the text, language and style, religious background, and theology. The additions are the apocryphal pieces attached to Daniel, such as Susanna's history, quoted in Greek on the title page. Daubney's study itself begins beyond these leaves.
trial-of-mary-blandy: William Roughead edited the Trial of Mary Blandy for a 1914 illustrated edition, dedicating the record of grim reality to Lord Dunsany. The front matter lays out the case as a table of dates. The trial fell on Tuesday, March 3, 1752, at Oxford, where Blandy was pictured in her cell in Oxford Castle. The contents list an indictment, opening speeches, and evidence from doctors. Only the title pages and this trial outline are present here, so the testimony itself does not appear.
turgenev-a-study:
Edward Garnett's Turgenev: A Study, copyright 1917, carries a foreword by Joseph Conrad written as a letter to the author. Conrad calls Turgenev a fortunate artist who found much in life yet missed bare justice. Garnett's study, he hopes, may help that justice arrive at last.

Conrad praises the English translator who missed none of Turgenev's delicate beauties, meaning the celebrated English edition Garnett introduced. Turgenev's creative work, he notes, covered about thirty years. Its depths, he argues, record the moral and intellectual unrest behind Russia's later upheavals. Women, Conrad insists, form the foundation of Turgenev's art, understood tenderly and reverently. The foreword alone makes the volume a document of two writers' friendship.
yolanda-maid-of-burgundy: Charles Major wrote this historical romance, published in 1905 with pictures by Charlotte Weber Ditzler. Pages present here hold a contents list covering ten chapters, but no chapter text. The titles open at a castle among crags and promise knights-errant. Yolanda is called a sorceress in one title, then a riddle in another. Duke Charles the Rash appears as a named figure. A race with the duke and a house under a wall close the list shown here.
